Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- Acute left-sided throbbing headache with visual aura, photophobia, nausea/vomiting; clinical impression most consistent with migraine with aura.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Sudden-onset left-sided throbbing headache beginning today at mid-day; preceded by zig-zag visual aura and blurred vision in both eyes.
- Associated symptoms: Photophobia (wearing sunglasses), nausea with two episodes of vomiting. Headache worsens with head/neck movement or leaning forward.
- Pertinent negatives: No fever, rash, speech difficulty, limb weakness, balance problems, neck stiffness, or recent head trauma. No breathlessness.
- Prior episodes: Similar headache a few weeks ago lasting ~2 days, improved with rest and analgesia.
- Past medical history: Denies chronic illnesses or prior migraine diagnosis.
- Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill (Microgynon) for 3 months; no regular analgesics reported.
- Allergies: Not discussed.
- Family history: Mother with migraines and hypothyroidism; no family brain tumors.
- Social / preventive: Works in stressful fashion industry; lives alone; denies smoking and alcohol; limited exercise.

Examination:
- No objective vitals provided; patient afebrile by history.
- No focal neurological deficits reported on review of systems.
- No skin rash or meningeal signs described.
- Physical examination otherwise not documented (teleconsult context).

Impression:
- Primary: Migraine with visual aura – highly likely given unilateral throbbing pain, preceding visual disturbance, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, similar prior episode, and positive family history.
- Alternative considerations (noted but less likely):
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – moderate risk because of new headache, positional worsening, recent estrogen OCP; no focal deficits.  
  • Intracranial mass – considered by patient; low likelihood due to acute presentation and normal neuro review.

Plan:
- Acute treatment: Advise use of strong analgesics (paracetamol or co-codamol) plus NSAID options (ibuprofen or naproxen) as tolerated.
- Self-management: Keep a headache diary to identify frequency and potential triggers.
- Follow-up: Review in 1 week to assess response and discuss prophylactic migraine therapy if headaches persist or increase.
- Safety-net advice: Seek urgent care if headache worsens or fails to improve over 2–3 days, develops new neurological symptoms (weakness, vision changes, speech problems), increasing neck pain, or uncontrolled vomiting.

Quality checks:

● Missing elements  
- Allergies explicitly unrecorded.  
- Objective vital signs and physical exam findings absent.  
- No documentation of weight/BMI or menstrual/ hormonal headache triggers.  
- Specific follow-up appointment date/time not arranged; no investigation plan if atypical course.

● Transcript vs DDx conflicts  
- None significant; both align on migraine as most likely diagnosis.

● Transcript quality  
- Clear history; limited examination due to likely telephone/virtual setting; no vitals recorded.
